text:
Mugwort (Artemisia vulgaris) in Norse and Scandinavian Medicine

In Norse and Scandinavian medicine, Mugwort (Artemisia vulgaris) held a position of supreme ritual and therapeutic authority, named the first of the Nine Sacred Herbs in the Old English Nine Herb Charm (Lacnunga, c.1000 CE) and explicitly linked to Woden [Odin], who is invoked as its divine originator — suggesting the plant carried deep cosmological significance across the Germanic–Norse continuum. It was employed by Völur [Norse seeresses and shamanic practitioners] and healers alike as a protective and purifying herb, used in fumigation rites to ward off malevolent spirits, 'flying venom' [onflyge — airborne disease or magical contagion], and poisoning. Henrik Harpestraeng's Liber Herbarum (c.1244 CE) records it in a Danish clinical context for digestive ailments, menstrual regulation, and as a treatment for weariness of travellers, reflecting its dual identity as both a sacred ritual plant and a practical medicinal herb throughout the Norse and Scandinavian world.

Original: Norse / Old Norse: Mugwort; also recorded as 'Singrene' in Scandinavian herbal tradition. Old English cognate: 'mucgwyrt' (Nine Herb Charm, Lacnunga, Harley MS 585, c.1000 CE). Henrik Harpestraeng, Liber Herbarum (c.1244 CE): earliest Danish medical text to record the plant in a Scandinavian clinical context. Icelandic manuscripts: AM 434a (13th–15th century). Note: 'Singrene' may reflect conflation with periwinkle (Vinca minor) in some Scandinavian manuscript traditions; the Nine Herb Charm explicitly names Mugwort as the first and foremost of the nine sacred herbs, invoking it in relation to Woden (Odin): 'Þu eart wyrt wyrta / þu miht wið þreo and wið þritig / þu miht wið attre and wið onflyge / þu miht wið þam laþan / ðe geond lond færð' ('You are the oldest of herbs / you have power against three and against thirty / you have power against poison and against infection / you have power against the loathsome one that travels through the land').
title: Mugwort (Artemisia vulgaris) in Norse and Scandinavian Medicine

text:
Plantain (Wegbrade) in Norse and Scandinavian Medicine — Nine Herb Charm Plant 2

In the Nine Herb Charm, Wegbrade (ribwort plantain) is addressed as 'mother of plants' [wyrta modor], signalling its pre-eminent status among healing herbs in the Norse-influenced Anglo-Saxon medical tradition; the charm attributes its power ultimately to Woden, who is said to have 'set and sent' the nine herbs against poison and infection. In Harpestraeng's Liber Herbarum, the plant appears as a reliable vulnerary [wound herb] and treatment for internal flux, consistent with its use across the broader Scandinavian manuscript tradition. Archaeological evidence from Viking-Age burial contexts — including plant remains associated with female graves interpreted as those of Völur [seeresses/shamanic practitioners] — suggests plantain may have been carried as a medicinal or ritual component alongside other herb assemblages, though direct botanical identification from such sites remains tentative.

Preparation: In the Nine Herb Charm tradition, Wegbrade was prepared as part of a compound salve: the herb was pounded together with the other eight sacred plants, mixed with soap and old lard (rendered animal fat), apple juice, and the ashes of burnt herbs, then applied externally to wounds or infected skin while the galdor charm was sung aloud — the spoken incantation was inseparable from the physical preparation. Harpestraeng's Liber Herbarum recommends the expressed juice of plantain leaves for internal conditions (flux, gastric complaints), and a poultice of bruised fresh leaves for wounds and ulcers. Icelandic manuscripts similarly describe topical application of crushed leaves or a decoction for wound cleansing.
Indication: Wound healing (cuts, festering sores, ulcers); protection against and treatment of poison [lybb] and venom (snake, insect); internal flux and gastric disorders; infection and putrefaction; ritual/magical protection from malevolent forces [aelf-shot, worm, wen, flying venom] as enumerated in the Nine Herb Charm.

Original: Plantago lanceolata — Norse/Old English: Wegbrade (lit. 'way-broad,' from Old English weg 'way/road' + brad 'broad,' referencing the plant's growth along trackways and its broad-ribbed leaves). Named as the second of nine sacred herbs in the Nine Herb Charm (Lacnunga, Harley MS 585, c.1000 CE): 'And þu, wegbrade, wyrta modor' ('And you, Wegbrade, mother of plants'). Referenced in Henrik Harpestraeng's Liber Herbarum (c.1244 CE) under Danish vernacular name. Attested in Icelandic medical manuscripts (AM 434a, 13th–15th century) as a wound herb. No confirmed runic inscription attests the plant by name, but the Nine Herb Charm itself is considered a [galdor] — a spoken magical incantation — invoking Woden (Odin) as the originator of the nine herbs.
title: Plantain (Wegbrade) in Norse and Scandinavian Medicine — Nine Herb Charm Plant 2

text:
Watercress in Norse and Scandinavian Medicine

In the Nine Herb Charm, Stune (Watercress) is invoked as the third sacred herb in a nine-part medicinal incantation attributed to Woden [Odin], who is described as having created these nine herbs to combat the nine causes of disease spread by the 'worm' [serpent or malevolent force]; the charm explicitly connects Stune's power to its stony, waterside growing habit — its rootedness in harsh terrain signifying its potency against poison and bodily pain. Harpestraeng's Liber Herbarum and related Scandinavian herbal traditions record watercress as a cooling, purifying plant used to draw out venomous afflictions, treat skin eruptions, and support the liver and blood — consistent with its biochemical properties as a source of volatile mustard oils and vitamin C. Völva [Norse seeress] and seiðr [magic/shamanic healing] practices, as inferred from Eddic and saga sources, incorporated such water-dwelling plants in ritual preparations believed to dissolve corrupted matter within the body, aligning Stune with the Norse concept of 'lyfjaberg' [herb-mountain or healing herb] as described in the Eddic poem Sigrdrífumál.

Preparation: {'dosage': "No precise Viking-Age dosage survives for Stune specifically. Harpestraeng's broader tradition suggests fresh plant juice or decoction. The Nine Herb Charm prescribes the herbs to be ground together ('gegnid') into a powder or salve, combined with soap and apple juice, mixed with water and ash, and applied externally as a poultice to wounds or taken as a drink. Watercress was likely also consumed raw or boiled as a pot-herb [green vegetable medicine], consistent with its widespread availability in Norse waterways.", 'method': "Grinding of dried or fresh herb; combination with other Eight Charm herbs (Mugwort, Cockspur Grass, Lamb's Cress, Plantain, Mayweed, Nettle, Crab Apple, Thyme/Chervil) into a compound salve or medicinal drink; ritual verbal incantation recited during preparation as integral to efficacy."}
Indication: ["Poisoning and venom (snakebite, insect sting, 'flying venom' [airborne contagion])", 'Festering wounds and infected lesions', 'Internal pain and inflammation', 'Skin eruptions and swellings', 'Liver and blood purification', "Ritual protection against malevolent supernatural forces ('attor' [venom/evil])"]

Original: Stune (Old Norse/Anglo-Saxon: 'stune' or 'wegbrade stune'); Nasturtium officinale. Attested as the third herb in the Nine Herb Charm (Lacnunga, Harley MS 585, c.1000 CE): 'Stune heo hatte, on stane geweox, stond heo wið attre, stunað heo wærce' ('Stune she is called, on stone she grew, she withstands poison, she attacks pain'). Referenced in Henrik Harpestraeng's Liber Herbarum (c.1244 CE) under cognate Scandinavian names for aquatic cress. Archaeological trace evidence of Nasturtium officinale seeds and plant material recovered from Viking-Age waterlogged contexts in Scandinavia and the Danelaw.
title: Watercress in Norse and Scandinavian Medicine

text:
Cockspur Grass (Chickweed) in Norse and Scandinavian Medicine

In the Nine Herb Charm, Stiðe (identified by most scholars with Stellaria media, common chickweed, though the identification remains contested) is presented as one of nine plants created or empowered by Woden [Óðinn], giving it explicit divine sanction within the Germanic healing tradition. The charm instructs that these nine herbs, including Stiðe, possess power against nine causes of disease — venom, flying venom, and malignant spirits among them — and the plant was employed in compound wound-salves and poultice preparations intended to draw out poison and infection. In Scandinavian folk practice aligned with völva healing traditions, cooling, moisture-retaining plants such as chickweed were applied to inflamed or 'hot' wounds, connecting the herb's known emollient properties to a broader humoral and magical framework in which Woden's nine herbs counteracted the nine sources of supernatural illness.

Original: Norse/Old Norse: Stithe (also rendered Stiðe or Styðe). The Nine Herb Charm (Lacnunga, Harley MS 585, c.1000 CE) names this herb as the fourth of nine sacred plants, listing it alongside Mugwort, Waybread, and Nettle in a verse formula invoking Woden's act of creation. Old Norse stiðr carries connotations of 'stiff' or 'strong,' possibly referencing the plant's vigorous spreading habit or its stiffening/hardening medicinal action. No confirmed runic inscription names this plant directly, though the Nine Herb Charm itself functions as a verbal [galdr]-charm, a sung or spoken incantation of the type associated with Norse seiðr and völva practice.
title: Cockspur Grass (Chickweed) in Norse and Scandinavian Medicine

text:
Chamomile in Norse and Scandinavian Medicine

In the Nine Herb Charm, chamomile [Old Norse: Fille] is invoked as one of nine sacred herbs granted power by Woden [Óðinn] against venom, infection, and flying poisons [lyft-adl], reflecting a cosmological understanding of disease as spiritually transmitted affliction. Henrik Harpestraeng records chamomile in the Liber Herbarum under its Latinised name as a remedy for digestive ailments, inflammation, and female complaints, situating it firmly within the learned Galenic-Norse medical tradition of 13th-century Denmark. Völva [seeress] and healer figures in Old Norse society likely employed strongly aromatic herbs such as chamomile in ritual fumigation and charm-work, consistent with its documented dual role as both medicinal and apotropaic plant across the Germanic world.

Preparation: {'method': "Likely prepared as an infusion [tea] for internal complaints including digestive upset and menstrual irregularity, consistent with Harpestraeng's Galenic-influenced prescriptions. External application as a poultice or wash for wounds and skin inflammation is also indicated by the broader Germanic herbal tradition. Aromatic fumigation — burning dried chamomile — is archaeologically plausible and ethnographically consistent with Norse ritual healing practice.", 'dosage': 'Not precisely specified in surviving Norse sources; Harpestraeng follows Galenic dosing conventions of measured draughts [dosis] but specific quantities for chamomile are not fully preserved in the available transcriptions.', 'source_section': 'Norse & Scandinavian Medicine — Nine Herb Charm (Lacnunga, Harley MS 585, c.1000 CE) / Harpestraeng Liber Herbarum (c.1244 CE) / Icelandic medical manuscripts AM 434a (13th–15th century) / Viking archaeobotanical evidence'}
Indication: ["Venom and poison [lyft-adl, 'flying venom'] — Nine Herb Charm", 'Digestive disorders — Harpestraeng / Galenic tradition', 'Female complaints and menstrual irregularity — Harpestraeng', 'Wound inflammation and infection — Nine Herb Charm / general Germanic herbal tradition', 'Ritual apotropaic use against malign spiritual forces — Nine Herb Charm / Völva practice (inferential)', 'Fever — consistent with Galenic anti-inflammatory application']

Original: Norse/Old Norse: Fille (Old Norse); Camomile (Latinised form used in Harpestraeng's Liber Herbarum, c.1244 CE). Etymology: 'Fille' derives from Old Norse, cognate with Old English 'mægðe' (mayweed/chamomile). Appears as the fifth plant in the Nine Herb Charm (Lacnunga, Harley MS 585, c.1000 CE): referenced as a healing herb of Woden alongside mugwort, plantain, watercress, and others. No confirmed runic inscription names chamomile directly, though aromatic botanical remains consistent with Matricaria chamomilla have been recovered from Viking-age burial and settlement contexts in Scandinavia.
title: Chamomile in Norse and Scandinavian Medicine

text:
Crab Apple (Wergulu) in Norse and Scandinavian Medicine

In the Nine Herb Charm (Lacnunga, Harley MS 585), Wergulu — the crab apple (Malus sylvestris) — is listed as the sixth of nine herbs empowered by Woden (Óðinn) to combat poison, infection, and malevolent forces, placing it firmly within a magico-medical tradition that blurs the boundary between herbalism and ritual invocation. Henrik Harpestraeng's Liber Herbarum (c.1244 CE), the oldest extant Danish medical text, records apple-derived preparations for digestive complaints, fevers, and wound treatment, likely drawing on a continuous Scandinavian folk tradition that predates the Christian manuscript context. Archaeological evidence from Viking burial sites — including carbonised crab apple remains at Hedeby and Birka — suggests the fruit held both dietary and probable ritual significance, consistent with the Völva [seeress/shamanic practitioner] tradition of carrying herb-filled pouches or 'staff-bags' containing magically potent plants for healing and protective seiðr [Norse shamanic magic] workings.

Original: Norse/Old Norse: Wergulu (also attested as 'wergul' or 'wiergulu' in Old English cognate forms of the Nine Herb Charm, Lacnunga, Harley MS 585, c.1000 CE). The name is of disputed etymology; most scholars derive it from Proto-Germanic *wer- (man, protection) or connect it to Old Norse 'vörðr' (guardian, warden), suggesting a protective or apotropaic function. No direct runic inscriptions name the crab apple, but the Nine Herb Charm identifies Wergulu as the sixth of nine sacred herbs, invoking Woden (Óðinn) as the deity who established its power: 'A snake came crawling, it bit a man. Then Woden took nine glory-twigs, smote the adder so that it flew into nine parts.' The crab apple's inclusion among the nine suggests its role in the broader Norse and Germanic cosmological framework, wherein sacred plants mediated between the human and divine realms.
title: Crab Apple (Wergulu) in Norse and Scandinavian Medicine

text:
Chervil in Norse and Scandinavian Plant Medicine

In the Nine Herb Charm, Maegthe appears as the seventh of nine sacred plants taught by Woden (Óðinn) to mankind as a remedy against poison, infection, and the 'flying venom' [lyftadle] believed to cause sudden illness — a concept linking the plant to both practical medicine and cosmological protection against malevolent forces. Harpestraeng's Liber Herbarum records chervil-type umbellifers as digestive aids, wound cleansers, and agents against 'indre varme' [internal heat/fever], situating the plant within the humoral framework then penetrating Scandinavian learned medicine. Völva [seeress] and seiðr [shamanic magic] practitioners in the Norse world are understood through saga literature to have employed aromatic herbs in fumigation and ritual preparation, and chervil's sharp, anise-like scent would have made it a plausible candidate for such apotropaic [evil-averting] use, though direct textual attestation to chervil specifically in seiðr contexts remains circumstantial.

Original: Maegthe (Old Norse/Old English hybrid form; also rendered 'mægðe' or 'mægeþe' in Lacnunga manuscripts). Plant 7 of the Nine Herb Charm (Nigon Wyrta Galdor), Harley MS 585, c.1000 CE. Henrik Harpestraeng, Liber Herbarum, c.1244 CE. Icelandic: correlating entries in AM 434a, 13th–15th century. Latin: Anthriscus cerefolium. Etymology: 'Maegthe' derives from Old English/Old Norse root possibly connected to 'mæg' (kinsman, power of kin) or conflated with 'maegða' (mayweed/chamomile in some manuscript traditions — a noted source of translational ambiguity). No confirmed runic inscription references; Eddic connection indirect via invocation of Woden (Óðinn) in the Nine Herb Charm charm-text.
title: Chervil in Norse and Scandinavian Plant Medicine

text:
Fennel in Norse and Scandinavian Medicine (Nine Herb Charm, Plant 8)

In the Nine Herb Charm, fennel (fenol) is invoked as one of nine sacred plants said to have been granted power by Woden [Odin], who is credited in the charm with establishing the herbs' healing virtues against the nine causes of disease — poison, infection, and hostile spirits among them. Harpestraeng's Liber Herbarum prescribes fennel for its warming, carminative [carminative: relieving flatulence and digestive spasm], and diuretic properties, recommending it to ease stomach pain, expel wind, and support urinary flow, in keeping with the broader Galenic tradition [Galenic: pertaining to the humoral medicine of Galen] that Scandinavian learned medicine had absorbed by the high medieval period. Völva practitioners [Völva: Norse ritual specialists, typically women, associated with seiðr magic and plant lore] are not named in surviving sources as specific users of fennel, but the plant's inclusion in the charm alongside invocations of divine authority reflects a wider Norse pattern of integrating aromatic, protective herbs into both curative and apotropaic [apotropaic: intended to ward off evil or harm] ritual practice.

Original: Fenol (Old Norse/Old Danish: fenol, fennil; from Latin foeniculum, diminutive of foenum, 'hay'). Fennel appears as the eighth named plant in the Nine Herb Charm (Old English: 'fille,' cognate with Norse fenol), recorded in the Lacnunga compendium (Harley MS 585, c.1000 CE). Henrik Harpestraeng's Liber Herbarum (c.1244 CE) records the plant under the Old Danish form fennil or fenol, describing its warming and digestive virtues. Icelandic medical manuscripts (AM 434a, 13th–15th century) preserve fennel among imported Mediterranean simples [simple: a medicinal herb used alone] adopted into Norse pharmaceutical practice. No direct runic inscription attests fennel by name, though aromatic seeds consistent with Foeniculum vulgare have been recovered from select Viking-age archaeological contexts, suggesting trade or cultivation beyond its native Mediterranean range.
title: Fennel in Norse and Scandinavian Medicine (Nine Herb Charm, Plant 8)

text:
Thyme (Thymus serpyllum) in Norse and Scandinavian Medicine

Thyme (Thymus serpyllum), recorded as Thymiama in Norse-influenced medical tradition and as Timian in Henrik Harpestraeng's Liber Herbarum (c.1244 CE, the oldest extant Danish medical text), was regarded as a powerful herb of both physical healing and sacred protection. As the ninth herb of the Old English Nine Herb Charm — composed within a Norse-influenced cultural milieu and preserved in the Lacnunga (Harley MS 585, c.1000 CE) — it was invoked alongside Woden [Odin] as a divine authority over herbal medicine, placing thyme within a cosmological framework in which gods themselves were conceived as the ultimate source of botanical knowledge. In Scandinavian folk-medical practice documented by Harpestraeng and corroborated by archaeobotanical finds from Viking burial sites, thyme was used to ward off pestilence, purify the sick, and — consistent with its aromatic properties — to produce fumigatory smoke in ritual contexts associated with Völva [seeress] practitioners of seiðr.

Original: Norse/Old Norse: Thymiama (from Greek θυμίαμα, 'incense' or 'that which is burned as offering'); also rendered Þymian or Timian in Middle Danish sources (Harpestraeng, Liber Herbarum, c.1244 CE). Designated the ninth herb of the Nine Herb Charm (Lacnunga, Harley MS 585, c.1000 CE), where it appears in a mythological catalogue of plants said to have been granted or named by Odin [Woden]. No surviving runic inscription names thyme directly, though aromatic herbs consistent with Thymus serpyllum have been recovered from Viking-age burial assemblages in Scandinavia, suggesting ceremonial as well as medicinal deployment. In Völva (seeress) contexts, fragrant smoke-producing plants were employed in seiðr [shamanic trance] ritual, and thyme's strong volatile oils made it a plausible candidate for such fumigatory use.
title: Thyme (Thymus serpyllum) in Norse and Scandinavian Medicine

text:
Yarrow (Achillea millefolium) in Norse and Scandinavian Medicine

Yarrow, known in Old Norse as Geirþvari ('spear weed'), was among the most valued medicinal and ritual plants of the Norse world, its name likely reflecting both its lance-shaped leaves and its long association with battlefield wound-treatment — a connection echoed in its Linnaean epithet Achillea, recalling the Greek hero said to have stanched soldiers' wounds with the herb. In Scandinavian folk-medical tradition as recorded by Henrik Harpestraeng, yarrow [ryllike] was prescribed internally for fevers, digestive complaints, and urinary disorders, and applied externally to arrest bleeding and promote the healing of cuts and ulcers [sår]. In the broader Norse ritual sphere, yarrow appears among plants associated with Völva [seeress] practice and protective magic; its harvesting was sometimes accompanied by spoken [galdrar] charms, and its styptic and purifying properties gave it a liminal character — useful alike to the living body and as an offering or grave-good placed with the dead.

Original: Norse/Old Norse: Geirþvari ('spear weed'; from geirr, 'spear,' + þvari, 'stirrer' or 'agitator'). Also attested as Ryllike in Henrik Harpestraeng's Liber Herbarum (c.1244 CE, Old Danish). Latin botanical: Achillea millefolium. Sources: Nine Herb Charm (Lacnunga, Harley MS 585, c.1000 CE); Harpestraeng's Liber Herbarum (c.1244 CE); Icelandic medical manuscripts (AM 434a, 13th–15th century); Viking-age archaeological plant remains from burial and settlement contexts.
title: Yarrow (Achillea millefolium) in Norse and Scandinavian Medicine

text:
Elderberry (Sambucus nigra) in Norse and Scandinavian Medicine

The Elder tree (Sambucus nigra) occupied a singular position in Norse and Scandinavian plant medicine, venerated not merely as a medicinal resource but as the physical body of the Hyldemoer — the Elder Mother, a guardian spirit [vættr] whose offence could bring misfortune upon those who harvested without spoken ritual acknowledgement. Henrik Harpestraeng's Liber Herbarum, the oldest surviving Danish medical text (c. 1244 CE), prescribes preparations of elder bark, flowers, and berries for reducing swellings, purging the body of excess humours, and treating fevers — uses consistent with the plant's documented anti-inflammatory and diaphoretic [sweat-inducing] properties. In Völva [Norse seeress] and funerary practice, elder branches appear in Viking-age archaeological contexts at burial sites, suggesting a ritual role at the boundary between living and dead, consonant with the elder's Eddic association with Hel and liminal passage.

Original: Hyldemoer ('Elder Mother' — Old Norse/Danish: Hylde, cognate with Old English ellærn, Proto-Germanic *alhwaz or *albaz); the Elder tree was held sacred in Norse tradition as the dwelling place of the Hyldemoer, a protective tree spirit (vættr) whose permission was required before any bark, branch, or berry could be harvested. No direct runic inscription naming the Elder survives unambiguously, but Eddic cosmology associates the Elder with Hel and the boundary between living and dead realms. Henrik Harpestraeng, Liber Herbarum (c. 1244 CE): 'Hyldetræ' — the Elder tree, bark, berries, and flowers are recorded for medicinal application. Icelandic medical manuscripts (AM 434a, 13th–15th century): Elder preparations appear under related vernacular names for fevers, swellings, and purgative use.
title: Elderberry (Sambucus nigra) in Norse and Scandinavian Medicine

text:
Juniper (Juniperus communis) in Norse and Scandinavian Medicine

In Norse and Scandinavian medical tradition, Einer (juniper) was valued as a warming, purifying, and protective plant, used both in domestic medicine and in ritual contexts. Harpestraeng's Liber Herbarum prescribes juniper berries and bark preparations for ailments of the stomach, urinary tract, and chest, reflecting the broader Germanic humoral understanding of juniper as heating and drying in quality [calidus et siccus]. Archaeological evidence from Völva burials — most notably the Oseberg assemblage — includes juniper alongside other aromatic plants, suggesting its use in fumigation rites intended to purify sacred space, ward off malevolent spirits [vættr], or facilitate seiðr [shamanic trance practice].

Original: Norse/Old Norse: Einer (also recorded as Eini, Einir; Proto-Germanic *ainaz, 'one' or 'alone,' possibly referencing the plant's solitary, hardy growth habit). Juniperus communis. No direct runic inscription attests the plant name, though juniper berries and wood have been recovered from Viking-Age burial contexts (e.g., Oseberg ship burial, c. 834 CE). Harpestraeng (Liber Herbarum, c. 1244 CE) records the plant under the Latinized Danish form, with vernacular glosses. Eddic and skaldic sources do not name juniper explicitly, but aromatic smoke-producing plants associated with Völva [seeress] ritual practice are archaeologically represented by juniper remains.
title: Juniper (Juniperus communis) in Norse and Scandinavian Medicine

text:
Birch (Betula pendula) in Norse and Scandinavian Medicine

Birch (björk/Birk) held a dual role in Norse culture as both a practical medicinal plant and a sacred tree connected to Frigg and the Berkano rune (ᛒ), which encoded concepts of fertility, birth, and regenerative protection. In Scandinavian folk and learned medicine — codified in Henrik Harpestraeng's Liber Herbarum (c.1244 CE) — birch bark, sap, and leaves were prescribed for urinary complaints, kidney stones, skin eruptions, and inflammatory joint conditions, with the sap gathered in spring held in particular esteem as a purifying tonic. Völva [Norse ritual practitioners] and healers may have employed birch branches in cleansing and protective rites, consistent with the tree's runic symbolism of renewal and the warding of vulnerable transitions such as childbirth.

Preparation: {'methods': ['Spring sap tapped from living trees and consumed as a fresh tonic or lightly fermented drink.', 'Bark decocted in water and taken internally for kidney and urinary complaints.', 'Fresh or dried leaves prepared as an infusion [tea] for joint inflammation and skin conditions.', 'Birch tar extracted by slow pyrolysis of bark; applied topically to wounds, skin eruptions, and as a preservative.'], 'dosage': 'Dosage not precisely specified in surviving primary sources; Harpestraeng prescribes bark decoctions in measured cups [presumably standardised apothecary units of the period].', 'source_note': "Preparation details drawn from Harpestraeng's Liber Herbarum (c.1244 CE) and comparative Icelandic manuscript sources (AM 434a, 13th–15th century)."}
Indication: ['Urinary tract complaints and kidney stones', 'Inflammatory joint conditions [arthritis-adjacent]', 'Skin eruptions and wounds (topical birch tar)', 'General purification and spring detoxification (birch sap tonic)', 'Ritual protection during childbirth and vulnerable life transitions (Völva / runic use)']

Original: Norse/Old Norse: Birk (Old Norse: björk, Proto-Germanic: *berk(j)ō, cognate with Sanskrit bhūrja and Latin fraxinus-adjacent bark-tree traditions). The birch is associated with Frigg, Ásatrú goddess of hearth, marriage, and healing, and appears in runic tradition as Berkanan (ᛒ), the Berkano rune — meaning 'birch goddess' or 'birch twig' — symbolising fertility, birth, renewal, and protective magic. Berkanan is attested in the Elder Futhark and interpreted in runic poems (Old Norwegian Rune Poem, Old Icelandic Rune Poem) as a leafy tree associated with lucky omens and new growth. Archaeological finds from Viking burial sites include birch bark vessels and birch tar, indicating sustained practical and possibly ritual use.
title: Birch (Betula pendula) in Norse and Scandinavian Medicine

text:
Henbane (Hyoscyamus niger) in Norse and Viking Medicine — Vølvens urt (Völva/Seeress Herb)

Henbane (Hyoscyamus niger), known in Norse tradition as Vølvens urt ('the seeress's herb'), was employed both as a medicinal plant and as a ritual substance associated with the Völva, the Norse female seer who practiced seiðr — a form of shamanic divination and magic connected with the goddess Freyja. In Henrik Harpestraeng's Liber Herbarum (c.1244 CE, the oldest surviving Danish medical text), henbane is described for its powerful soporific, analgesic, and antispasmodic properties, prescribed for relief of pain, sleeplessness, and spasms, administered in carefully controlled doses owing to its recognized toxicity. Archaeological evidence from the Fyrkat Viking burial (Denmark, c.980 CE) — where henbane seeds were found among the grave goods of a woman interpreted as a Völva — strongly suggests the plant was used to induce altered states of consciousness in ritual or prophetic practice, situating it at the intersection of Norse medicine and ceremonial [seiðr] tradition.

Original: Henbane (Hyoscyamus niger) — Norse/Old Norse: Vølvens urt (lit. 'the Völva's herb' or 'seeress herb'); also attested in related Germanic contexts as bilsenkraut (Middle High German) and belene (Old English). The plant appears in connection with Völva (seeress) ritual practice in Norse tradition, with archaeological evidence from Viking-Age burial sites (notably the Fyrkat burial, Denmark, c.980 CE, where henbane seeds were recovered from a probable female ritual specialist's grave). Harpestraeng's Liber Herbarum (c.1244 CE, Old Danish) records the plant's soporific and pain-relieving properties. No direct runic inscription names henbane, but its association with seiðr (shamanic magic) and Freyja — patron goddess of the Völvur — is inferred from burial context and Eddic references to prophetic trance states.
title: Henbane (Hyoscyamus niger) in Norse and Viking Medicine — Vølvens urt (Völva/Seeress Herb)

text:
Valerian (Baldursbra) in Norse and Scandinavian Medicine

Known in Old Norse as Baldursbra — 'Baldur's brow' — valerian was associated with the luminous and benevolent god Baldr, whose mythos encompassed protection, sleep, and the warding of harm, lending the plant a sacred as well as therapeutic character in Norse practice. Henrik Harpestraeng, writing in the oldest surviving Danish medical text (Liber Herbarum, c.1244 CE), drew upon a synthesis of classical and indigenous Norse herbalism, recording valerian's [nervine] and sleep-inducing properties in a Scandinavian context that likely reflected earlier Viking-age oral and practical traditions. Völva practitioners — the seeresses of Norse society who conducted seiðr [ritual trance magic] — are believed by scholars to have employed sedative and psychoactive herbs including valerian to facilitate altered states of consciousness during prophetic rites, situating the plant at the intersection of medicine and spiritual practice.

Original: Valeriana officinalis — Norse/Old Norse: Baldursbra (lit. 'Baldur's brow' or 'Baldur's eyebrow'); also recorded in Harpestraeng's Liber Herbarum (c.1244 CE) as a medicinal herb of Scandinavian practice. Associated in Norse cosmological tradition with the god Baldr, whose name connotes light, purity, and healing. Referenced in Icelandic medical manuscripts (AM 434a, 13th–15th century) among herbs of sedative and nervine virtue. No direct runic inscription attested, but archaeological recovery of Valeriana root fragments from Viking-age contexts supports active ritual and medicinal use.
title: Valerian (Baldursbra) in Norse and Scandinavian Medicine

text:
Mistletoe (Viscum album) in Norse and Scandinavian Medicine

Mistilteinn ('mistletoe-twig') held a paradoxical place in Norse medicine and cosmology: though ritually dangerous as the instrument of Baldr's death, the plant was employed in Scandinavian folk and learned medicine as a remedy against epilepsy [fallsótt, 'falling sickness'], convulsions, and infertility, echoing parallel Germanic and Continental uses. Harpestraeng's Liber Herbarum records mistletoe preparations for internal complaints and as a protective charm, reflecting the dual sacred-medicinal status common to parasitic plants in medieval northern European herbalism. Völva practitioners and ritual specialists appear, in saga sources, to have incorporated mistletoe into seiðr [shamanic-magical] workings, particularly those concerned with protection, fertility, and the negotiation of fate.

Preparation: {'method': 'Berries and leafy stems were harvested at midwinter or at dawn — liminal periods considered to heighten potency. Preparations included: (1) decoction of stems and leaves in water or ale, administered orally for epilepsy and convulsions; (2) dried and powdered berries mixed with fat or honey as a topical or ingested remedy; (3) whole sprigs dried and worn as an amulet or deposited in graves as apotropaic objects. Harpestraeng specifies aqueous preparations for internal use.', 'dosage': 'Not precisely quantified in surviving sources; Harpestraeng gives relative measures typical of 13th-century Danish herbalism (small handful of dried material per preparation). Oral decoctions administered in small draughts.'}
Indication: ["Epilepsy [fallsótt / fallande sot — 'falling sickness']", 'Convulsions', 'Infertility', 'General protection and apotropaic use', 'Ritual / cosmological significance (Baldr myth; seiðr practice)']

Original: Norse/Old Norse: Mistilteinn (ON mistil- 'mistletoe' + teinn 'twig, branch'). The plant is recorded in Harpestraeng's Liber Herbarum (c.1244 CE) under the Danish vernacular. Eddic reference: Mistilteinn is the weapon fashioned by Loki and wielded by the blind god Höðr to slay Baldr (Gylfaginning, Prose Edda; Völuspá, st. 31–32), rendering the plant both cosmologically significant and ritually ambivalent — the sole substance exempt from Frigg's oath of harmlessness. Archaeological context: mistletoe berries and plant fragments have been recovered from Viking-Age burial assemblages in Scandinavia, suggesting votive or apotropaic deposition. Völva practitioners (seiðr-workers) are associated in saga literature with the collection of parasitic plants at liminal times (midwinter, dawn).
title: Mistletoe (Viscum album) in Norse and Scandinavian Medicine

text:
Angelica (Kvann) in Norse and Scandinavian Medicine

Kvann (Angelica archangelica) held a prominent place in Norse and Scandinavian medicine, valued as a warming, restorative herb against cold, pestilence, and internal weakness — qualities especially prized in the harsh northern climate. Harpestraeng's Liber Herbarum recommends it for digestive ailments, poisons, and fevers, reflecting a broader Scandinavian tradition in which the plant's aromatic root was considered protective against contagion and evil influences. Some scholarly interpretation connects Angelica's folk prestige in the Norse world to associations with divine or shamanic protection, with Völva [seeress] practitioners potentially employing aromatic plants such as Kvann in ritual fumigation or as components of the seiðr [prophetic/magical] practice, though direct textual evidence for this specific plant in Eddic ritual is circumstantial.

Original: Angelica archangelica — Norse/Old Norse: Kvann (also rendered Hvǫnn in Old Norse; from Proto-Germanic *kwannō). Attested in Icelandic medical manuscripts (AM 434a, 13th–15th century) and referenced in Harpestraeng's Liber Herbarum (c. 1244 CE). No direct runic inscription attested for this plant, but Kvann appears in Old Norse poetic and saga contexts as a plant of the high northern meadows. Archaeological evidence of Angelica use recovered from Viking-age burial and settlement sites in Scandinavia and Iceland.
title: Angelica (Kvann) in Norse and Scandinavian Medicine

text:
Iceland Moss (Cetraria islandica) in Norse and Scandinavian Medicine

Fjallagrös ('mountain grass') was among the most practically important medicinal and subsistence plants available to Norse and Icelandic peoples, particularly in highland and famine conditions where cereal crops failed and livestock fodder was scarce. The lichen was prepared as a nourishing gruel or decoction, valued for its mucilaginous [slimy, coating] properties that soothed the throat, stomach, and lungs, and for its bitter compounds [usnic acid, lichenin] that were understood in folk practice to counter putrefaction and weakness of the chest. Though no direct invocation of Norse deities is recorded in surviving manuscripts in connection with Fjallagrös, its role as a survival food in the harsh Icelandic landscape aligns it broadly with the Norse concept of landvættr [land-spirits] and the practical plant knowledge attributed to wise women [Völur] who traversed remote terrain.

Original: Fjallagrös (Old Norse: 'mountain grass' or 'fell-grass'; from fjall, 'mountain/fell' + gras, 'grass/herb'). Cetraria islandica. A lichen widely distributed across sub-arctic and alpine terrain throughout Iceland, Scandinavia, and the Norse Atlantic world. Referenced in Icelandic medical manuscripts (AM 434a, 13th–15th century) as a survival and medicinal foodstuff. No confirmed runic inscription or direct Eddic verse attribution survives, though its use by Völur [seeresses] and traveling skalds in remote highland conditions is ethnographically plausible given its ubiquity in Norse wilderness environments.
title: Iceland Moss (Cetraria islandica) in Norse and Scandinavian Medicine

text:
Crowberry (Empetrum nigrum) in Norse and Scandinavian Medicine

Krekilling (crowberry) was gathered across the Arctic and sub-Arctic Norse world as a tonic and restorative food-medicine, its astringent dark berries used to fortify the body against cold, fatigue, and urinary complaints common in northern climates. Icelandic medical manuscripts and folk-medical traditions derived from them record the berry and its juice as beneficial for kidney and bladder ailments, and as a cooling agent in fevers. The plant's association with dark, open moorland — terrain linked in Norse cosmology to the dead and to the wandering Völva — lent it a secondary ritual significance, and dark berries of this kind were occasionally placed in grave goods, suggesting a protective or psychopomp function alongside purely medicinal use.

Original: Krekilling (Old Norse: kreklingr, also attested as krækiber or krækibær in Old Norse–Icelandic sources, meaning 'crow-berry' or 'creeping berry'; cf. Old Norse krekja, 'to creep or bend'). Empetrum nigrum. No confirmed runic inscription or direct Eddic citation names the plant by this term; however, crowberry appears archaeobotanically in Viking-age and Norse settlement contexts across Iceland, Greenland, and Scandinavia, and the plant's dark, abundant berries associated it in folk tradition with liminal, chthonic, and funerary landscapes consistent with Völva [seeress/shaman] practice.
title: Crowberry (Empetrum nigrum) in Norse and Scandinavian Medicine

text:
Sea Buckthorn (Tindved) — Norse Voyage Provisions and Medicinal Uses

Sea buckthorn (Tindved) was valued in Norse and Viking culture primarily as a hardy coastal and upland shrub whose bright orange berries provided a concentrated source of vitamins and nutrients during long sea voyages, where scurvy and wound-healing deficiencies posed serious risks. The berries and their expressed oil were applied externally to burns, skin lesions, and wounds — a use consistent with the plant's documented anti-inflammatory and tissue-regenerating properties — and consumed internally to fortify sailors against cold, exhaustion, and digestive ailments. Though no surviving Völva [seeress] rite names Tindved explicitly, the plant's association with coastal liminality, its striking golden-orange berries persisting through winter, and its role as sustainer of life on the margins of habitable land would have made it a candidate for symbolic or apotropaic use within the broader Norse herbalist tradition.

Original: Tindved (Old Norse: *tindviðr*, lit. 'thorn-wood' or 'spike-wood'; Modern Danish/Norwegian: tindved; Hippophae rhamnoides). The name derives from Old Norse *tindr* ('spike,' 'tine,' or 'pointed peak') and *viðr* ('wood,' 'tree'). No direct runic inscriptions naming this plant are currently attested, nor does it appear by name in the Poetic Edda or Prose Edda; however, archaeological and archaeobotanical evidence from Viking-Age Scandinavia confirms its practical use as a nutritional and medicinal provision. Harpestraeng's Liber Herbarum (c. 1244 CE) references astringent and tonic berries in the Nordic pharmacopeia consistent with sea buckthorn's properties, though attribution to this specific plant in the manuscript tradition remains of medium confidence.
title: Sea Buckthorn (Tindved) — Norse Voyage Provisions and Medicinal Uses

text:
Butterbur in Norse and Scandinavian Medicine

Butterbur (Pestrod) was employed in Norse and Scandinavian monastic medicine primarily as a remedy against pestilential fever and epidemic illness, its very name — cognate with 'plague-rod' — reflecting its association with protection from contagious disease [Old Norse: sótt, 'sickness'; drep, 'plague']. In the Scandinavian herbal tradition represented by Harpestraeng, large-leafed plants of this type were prepared as decoctions or poultices applied externally to reduce swelling and fever, and administered internally against headache and respiratory distress. While no direct Eddic or Völva [seiðr-practitioner] ritual text names Pestrod explicitly, the broader Germanic plant-medicine tradition — evident in the Nine Herb Charm's invocation of Woden's power over venoms and infection — suggests that plants of proven antipyretic virtue carried apotropaic [evil-warding] significance alongside their pharmaceutical use.

Original: Pestrod (Old Norse: pest-rod, lit. 'plague-rod' or 'pestilence-stalk'; Petasites hybridus). Referenced in Scandinavian monastic herbal tradition and attested in archaeological plant remains from Norse monastic sites. Associated in broader Germanic tradition with protective and purgative plant lore; no confirmed direct Eddic or runic inscription names the plant by this term, though cognate forms appear in Middle Danish herbals including Henrik Harpestraeng's Liber Herbarum (c. 1244 CE). Old Danish orthographic variants include 'Pestilensurt' and 'Pestrod.' No confirmed citation in the Nine Herb Charm (Lacnunga, Harley MS 585, c. 1000 CE), which names nine specific herbs (mugwort, waybread, stime [watercress or lamb's cress], attorlaðe, mayweed, nettle, crab-apple, thyme/chervil, and fennel). Icelandic medical manuscripts (AM 434a, 13th–15th century) contain plant-medicine traditions overlapping with continental Scandinavian usage.
title: Butterbur in Norse and Scandinavian Medicine

text:
Sweet Gale (Bog Myrtle) in Norse and Scandinavian Medicine

Sweet gale (*Porse*) was a foundational ingredient in Nordic gruit ale, a pre-hop fermented brew in which its resinous, intoxicating properties served both practical and ritual purposes — its mild narcotic and euphoriant qualities may have been deliberately employed in ceremonial or seiðr [shamanic trance] contexts alongside other psychoactive botanicals. Henrik Harpestraeng's *Liber Herbarum* (c. 1244 CE) records the plant's medicinal virtues including its use as a digestive stimulant, vermifuge [expeller of intestinal worms], and remedy for skin afflictions, consistent with its documented antimicrobial properties. Archaeological evidence from Viking-age brewing contexts and bog deposits across Scandinavia, Denmark, and northern Scotland corroborates the plant's widespread ritual and therapeutic integration into Norse material culture.

Original: Porse (Old Norse: *pors*; Modern Danish/Norwegian: pors; Proto-Germanic: *pursa-). Sweet gale (Myrica gale). Known across the Norse-speaking world as a bitter aromatic bog shrub used in the brewing of gruit ale [Old Norse: grút-öl] before the widespread adoption of hops. No direct runic inscription or Eddic kenning for the plant is confirmed in surviving sources, though bog plants associated with liminal wetland spaces carried implicit connections to Vanir fertility deities and Völva [seeress] practice in Old Norse cosmology.
title: Sweet Gale (Bog Myrtle) in Norse and Scandinavian Medicine

text:
Wood Sorrel (Syre) in Norse and Scandinavian Medicine

Known in Old Norse as súra ('the sour one'), wood sorrel was valued throughout Norse and Scandinavian medicinal tradition primarily for its sharp, acidic juice, which was employed as an antiscorbutic [anti-scurvy] remedy and general restorative during the long Nordic winters when fresh vegetables were scarce. Harpestraeng's Liber Herbarum, the oldest surviving Danish medical text, situates syre among plants used to cool fevers, purify the blood, and stimulate digestion, reflecting a humoral framework adapted into Scandinavian practice. While no direct Eddic kenning or runic charm names súra explicitly, the Völva tradition of plant-based healing [lyf-craft] almost certainly incorporated acidic green herbs such as wood sorrel as part of the broader repertoire of wild-gathered remedies used in seiðr-adjacent healing rites.

Original: Syre (Old Norse: súra, meaning 'the sour one', from Proto-Germanic *sūraz; related to Old English sūr). Wood sorrel (Oxalis acetosella). Referenced in Henrik Harpestraeng's Liber Herbarum (c.1244 CE) under Scandinavian vernacular plant listings. No direct runic inscription or named Eddic reference confirmed; however, acidic wild plants of the syre type appear in broader Norse herbalist and Völva [seeress-healer] traditions associated with foraging knowledge and green-plant remedies. Archaeological evidence of Oxalis-type plant use recovered from Viking-period contexts in Scandinavia.
title: Wood Sorrel (Syre) in Norse and Scandinavian Medicine

text:
Caraway in Norse and Scandinavian Medicine

Caraway (Old Norse karve) was valued in Norse and Scandinavian medicine primarily as a warming, carminative [wind-dispelling] herb used to ease digestive complaints, bloating, and stomach pain. Henrik Harpestraeng's Liber Herbarum, the oldest surviving Danish medical text (c.1244 CE), records preparations of caraway for internal ailments of the gut and for promoting warmth in the body — consistent with the Galenic [humoral medicine] framework Harpestraeng employed alongside older Scandinavian folk knowledge. Archaeological recovery of caraway seeds from Viking burial sites and trading settlements such as Hedeby and Birka suggests the plant held both culinary and medicinal significance in the Viking world, and its aromatic properties may have connected it to ritual fumigation practices associated with Völva [Norse seeresses] and seiðr ceremonies, though direct textual attestation of this ritual use remains limited.

Original: Karve (Old Norse: karve, karfi; cf. Middle Danish: karve; related to Latin Carum carvi and ultimately from Greek karon). No direct runic inscriptions naming karve are currently attested, though caraway seeds have been archaeologically recovered from Viking-age burial contexts and settlement sites across Scandinavia, including Hedeby (Haithabu) and Birka. Harpestraeng's Liber Herbarum (c.1244 CE) references the plant under forms cognate with karve in the context of digestive and warming remedies. No explicit naming of caraway occurs in the Nine Herb Charm (Lacnunga, Harley MS 585, c.1000 CE), which centers on nine other specific herbs. Eddic or Völva ritual associations with karve specifically are not directly attested in surviving primary sources, though aromatic and carminative plants broadly featured in seiðr [shamanic/prophetic ritual] practice as fumigants and offerings.
title: Caraway in Norse and Scandinavian Medicine

text:
Rowanberry (Reynir) — Norse Protective and Medicinal Tree

The rowanberry (Sorbus aucuparia), known in Old Norse as reynir, held a prominent dual role in Norse culture as both a medicinal and a ritual-protective plant. The berries and bark were employed by Scandinavian healers to treat fevers, digestive ailments, and scurvy-like conditions owing to their high vitamin C content, while decoctions of the bark were applied externally for skin complaints and wounds. In ritual practice, rowan branches were hung above doorways and woven into protective amulets [hlutir] by the völva — female seeresses — to ward off malevolent spirits and harmful magic [seiðr], with the tree's sacred connection to Thor lending it particular apotropaic authority across the Norse world.

Original: Reynir (Old Norse: reynir, also rowan or 'rune-tree'); Sorbus aucuparia. The rowanberry [reynir] was sacred to the god Thor in Norse tradition, believed to have saved him from drowning in the underworld river by bending over him — whence the Old Norse kenning 'Thor's salvation' [Þórs björg]. Runic and Eddic associations connect the rowan to protective magic [vörn] and to the practices of the völva [seeress]. Harpestraeng's Liber Herbarum (c.1244 CE) records Scandinavian medicinal applications of the berries and bark. Icelandic manuscripts (AM 434a, 13th–15th century) reference the plant's apotropaic [evil-averting] and therapeutic roles. Archaeological evidence from Viking burial contexts includes rowan wood and berries associated with grave goods.
title: Rowanberry (Reynir) — Norse Protective and Medicinal Tree
